data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The single domain expert will remain more reliable because the checklist merely formalizes a subset of expertise, and the 'reliability' of the panel is an illusion of consistency that fails on the 'edge cases' which actually determine the objective outcome.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The task is highly routine with a finite, known set of failure modes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The expert is prone to high-frequency 'lapse' errors (e.g., forgetting to check a valve).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The checklist is comprehensive enough to cover 99% of all historical failure modes.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Reliability in complex, verifiable tasks is not the absence of simple errors, but the presence of 'deep' detection. The expert's intuition is a compressed representation of a high-dimensional state-space. A checklist is a low-dimensional projection. The panel's reliability is 'shallow'; they achieve consistency by ignoring any signal not explicitly listed. The expert wins because they detect 'unlisted' critical variables that are objectively verifiable but procedurally invisible (SCR_001).","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
